To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the majority of the dark matter in the Universe can be made up of black holes that originated from a single scalar field model of inflation with polynomial potential.

(i) the majority of dark-matter black holes may have been produced during a single-field inflation with a quartic polynomial inflationary potential and that (ii) the stochastic gravitational waves generated by this inflationary scenario could be detectable by future space-based observatory missions.
the abundance of primordial black holes in a single-field model is bounded from above by the dark matter abundance and that this upper bound may be tested by gravitational wave experiments.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question whether the primordial black hole dark matter hypothesis is testable by gravitational wave astronomy.
the interplay between inflation, primordial black holes, and gravitational waves.
the question whether the abundance of black holes in our Universe can be understood in terms of a simple single-field model of slow-roll inflation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a large black hole fraction of dark matter in combination with a polynomial inflation model is in tension with the current observational constraints.

primordial black holes as a dark matter candidate can only be considered if the primordial tensor-to-scalar ratio is large, r > ~ 0.01, and the primordial scalar power spectrum is blue, n_s > ~ 1, which would also be in agreement with the observed large scale structure.
primordial black holes as the main constituent of dark matter can be ruled out as a consequence of the current observational constraints.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a single-field model with a polynomial potential may explain both the dark matter abundance and the stochastic background of gravitational waves.
primordial black hole dark matter can be produced in a single-field inflationary model, provided the potential has a sufficiently large quartic term.
a dark matter abundance of black holes of order 1 can only be obtained if the tensor-to-scalar ratio is of the same order or larger.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the abundance of black holes in the early Universe is a generic prediction of inflation, which is testable by the next generation of gravitational wave detectors.
the dark matter abundance of black holes is tightly constrained by the amplitude and the shape of the primordial tensor power spectrum.
the abundance of primordial black holes in a single-field polynomial inflationary model is tightly linked to the tensor-to-scalar ratio.
